declared.title: Implanting rich autobiographical false memories: Meta-analysis for forensic practice and judicial judgment making
declared.venue: International Journal of Clinical and Health Psychology
declared.foundIn: Europe PMC search « "misinformation effect" AND ("meta-analysis" OR "meta-analytic") » (2026-11-23)

population: children and adults in 30 lab studies (simulation designs) that tried to implant rich false autobiographical memories; countries not listed

findings.text: Across 30 studies, rich false memories were implanted in more than a trivial share of people; the authors' d compares that rate with zero, not two groups

support.sentence: The results revealed a significant, positive, generalizable (the lower limit for the 80% credibility value was d = 1.13), and more than large mean effect size (d = 1.43[1.33, 1.53]) for the implanting of false memory.

findings.text: Compared with not implanting, the average chance of implanting a rich false memory was about even, as each study coded it, and it varied widely between studies

support.sentence: In short, the probability of implanting false memories was 50% i.e., a common effect.
support.readBy: memory-rewritten reviser, 2026-11-26: PMC10126919, Results (success against failure, p–q)

findings.text: Rates were similar in minors and in adults (groups compared: age was not manipulated)

support.sentence: A similar effect for memory implantation was observed in both the underage (d = 1.44[1.29, 1.59]), and in adults (d = 1.36[1.22, 1.50]).

limits: its d is a Cohen's h of the rate against a constant (zero), not a difference between two groups: never shown as « large »
the authors: effect sizes « so extraordinarily high that it was highly probable they had been overestimated »; no design separated a memory from going along
pools very different procedures (false narratives, doctored photos, true events with false details), all lab simulations
same coding debate as Scoboria 2017: what counts as a « rich » false memory
